ch07 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Editor Jorge Gracia's preface frames The Passion as a phenomenon that stirs people too deeply for indifference (a minister's fatal heart attack in a Brazilian cinema, reviews ranging from zero to five stars) and argues its religious stakes give its questions more bite than those of The Matrix or The Lord of the Rings. It lays out the book's five controversies: whether Christ had to suffer violently and what atonement means, whether the film is anti-Semitic, how faith relates to truth and to reading the Gospels as God's word, why Christ was killed, and whether Judas can be morally responsible for a betrayal God foreknew and redemption required. Gracia insists the collection takes no side and offers only a point of departure.

chapters.file: ch08 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
ch09 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: McInerny argues Gibson's film works like Kierkegaard's indirect communication: its shocking graphic realism, against the tamed stations of the cross and serene crucifixes of Catholic churches, targets nominal Christians and forces each viewer to hear Jesus's 'I want you' and confront the scandal of the Incarnation rather than domesticate it. He reads the film alongside Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions as embroidery with no meaning apart from the Gospels, and invokes Aquinas on the Eucharist as the continuing memorial of the passion in which Christ is hidden under bread and wine. The film is 'a sign of contradiction' that, like Nietzsche's self-declared Antichrist, divides humanity into acceptance or rejection, so that efforts to keep religion within the bounds of reason alone must distort it.

chapters.file: ch10 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
ch11 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Wrathall defends the film's violence by contrasting Fra Angelico's serene Descent from the Cross with Corinth's Red Christ and Gibson's Gethsemane rebuke ('You could not watch even one hour with me'), arguing the gore resists rationalizing Christ's suffering into an economy of exchange, as Camus's Father Paneloux in The Plague insists true faith must not. Drawing on Pascal's instrumental reason, Heidegger, and Merleau-Ponty, he develops a 'world-disclosive' account of faith: the tall-table scene between Mary and the young carpenter Jesus shows that new practices train new perception, and film reaches the body directly in ways written description cannot. He closes by faulting Gibson for pessimism: Christ's world looks as God-forsaken and demon-haunted as Judas's, closer to Dostoevsky's ascetic Father Ferapont than to a world made new.

chapters.file: ch12 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Walls argues the controversy lies not in the gore but in who died on the cross and why, and shows Gibson weaving the three classic atonement theories: Christ crushing the serpent in Gethsemane as the Christus-Victor ransom (with Augustine's mousetrap image), the Isaiah 53 scourging and Gibson's own hand driving the nail as Anselm-style penal substitution in which the innocent dies so the guilty Barabbas in each of us goes free, and the transformed characters (Mary Magdalene, Simon of Cyrene, the good thief, the kneeling soldier) as Abelard's moral influence. Against Kant's charge that atonement is a superstitious substitute for moral transformation, he cites Swinburne and Quinn: pleading the atonement requires repentance, and the tens of thousands of reported conversions and confessions show it transforms lives. He concludes that any adequate account needs all three theories, objective payment and subjective transformation alike, and that atonement aims at mercy and reconciliation rather than retribution.

chapters.file: ch13 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Taliaferro, writing as a personalist, worries that Gibson's relentless focus on torture eclipses the whole person of Christ: like torture victims losing peripheral vision, viewers lose sight of his teaching, healings, nonviolence, and resurrection, and the satisfaction-theology framing risks relishing redemptive suffering itself. His reconciliation thought-experiment (Patricia's betrayal of Kris and the God-man who resurrects the murdered child) argues that the resurrection, not the passion alone, completes at-one-ment, since no amount of suffering can undo past wrong. He contrasts Gandalf's laughing return in The Return of the King with a Gibson Jesus who could not plausibly laugh after rising, and invokes Scheler's St. Francis, who loves the wholeness behind sickness rather than the sickness, to urge that the film's intensity edges out a life-affirming view of persons as irreducibly valuable in themselves.

chapters.file: ch14 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Irwin defends the film's violence aesthetically: beauty (Michelangelo's Pietà) distracts from moral truth rather than serving it, and Aristotle's Poetics fits the film neither as tragedy (a flawless Christ cannot fall through hamartia, and a good man's fall from prosperity is 'repulsive', so no catharsis explains why we watch) nor as the Plato-banned spectacle that inflames the passions, since it leaves viewers numb rather than belligerent. Instead he applies Cynthia Freeland's four features of the cinematic sublime, drawn from Burke and Kant: the flogging scenes, the grotesque Satan clutching his deformed child, Judas harried by demon-children to suicide, and even the Aramaic and Latin subtitles produce the pain-pleasure conflict, overwhelming vastness, and jolt from feeling to moral reflection that make the experience sublime. The violence is thus justified as Gibson's deliberate delivery of the sublime, provided viewers leave fear at the gates.

chapters.file: ch15 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Lawler charges that Gibson's atonement theology, in which the more barbaric the torture the greater the redemption, imprisons Christianity at the stage of Hegel's 'Unhappy Consciousness', where an infinite God is sundered from abject sinful humanity and a priestly mediator is needed. Reading the film through the master-slave dialectic (impotent master Pilate versus the dignified slave Simon of Cyrene; the world of separate egos as Hobbes's war of all against all), he argues that what dies on the cross is the separate ego itself, and that what rises is Geist, the 'I' that is 'We' of the loving human community. Against Tertullian's credo quia absurdum, and using Pascal's 'heart has its reasons' alongside Hegel's dialectical reason, he reads 'you are gods' and the prodigal son as teaching every person's essential divinity, so the film's own art (the Mater Dolorosa, our identification with the flesh-and-blood Jesus) implicitly undermines the separatist theology Gibson intends.

chapters.file: ch16 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
ch17 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Wartenberg recounts a Mount Holyoke panel where a New Testament historian, a scholar of Jewish mysticism, campus ministers, and a film theorist effectively saw different movies, and proposes that the film itself divides into 'The Passion of the Condemnation' (where a humane, tormented Pilate caves to bloodthirsty Jewish crowds, complete with the Matthew 27:25 blood-guilt line left untranslated for American test audiences) and 'The Passion of the Crucifixion' (the two-hour torture that true believers experience as their God's willing sacrifice, overwhelming everything before it). He then explains the split audience through cinema's photographic verisimilitude: just as D.W. Griffith's The Birth of a Nation used documentary-style realism to pass Klan apologetics off as history, Gibson's brutally realistic violence lends his slanted, Emmerich-inflected narrative the authority of fact. He rejects the postmodernist consolation that all readings are equally valid, insisting believers were manipulated by the medium's false trustworthiness.

chapters.file: ch18 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Kurtz, the secular humanist, argues the film is a political weapon of the Religious Right (O'Reilly, Dobson, Gingrich) that presents fantasy as fact: Gibson claims fidelity to the Gospels while borrowing torture scenes such as the bridge plunge and the savage flogging from Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions, whitewashing the historical Pilate, and erasing that Jesus, Mary, and the disciples were themselves Jews. Applying historical criticism, he contends the Gospels are anonymous, second- and third-hand missionary propaganda written forty to seventy years after Jesus, shaped by the rivalry between rabbinic Judaism and Gentile-seeking Jewish Christianity and canonized politically at Nicaea under Constantine. He concludes by defending the freedom of inquiry, skeptical scrutiny of all sacred texts, and the First Amendment's separation of church and state against the film's power to inflame anti-Semitism and the American culture war.

chapters.file: ch19 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Corlett applies the ethics of racism, due process, responsibility, and punishment to the film: he argues The Passion is not racist because it depicts dissenting Sanhedrin members, the supportive Simon of Cyrene, and the Jewish Mary and Jesus, so blame falls on individual wrongdoers like Caiaphas rather than on Jews as a group, and audiences' misreadings are not the artist's fault. He catalogs the violations of due process (guilty-until-proven-innocent before the Sanhedrin, beatings en route to the hearing, the swap for the convicted killer Barabbas) and the failure to separate religious from civil authority. On punishment he defends a principle of proportionality and desert: Jesus's innocence made his torture and execution unjust, but abuse does not negate proper use, so the film gives no argument against capital punishment per se while giving evildoers who escape earthly justice their deserts only if God is just.

chapters.file: ch20 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Bronson argues Gibson's fixation on Jesus's suffering is not a Christian oddity but a deeply Jewish mystical one: using William James's four marks of mystical experience (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity), he reads the Gethsemane opening, where Jesus crushes Satan's serpent and receives a vision of the Father, as a classic mystical trial in the line of Moses at Sinai, Daniel's chariot-throne vision, Elijah's fiery ascent, John the Baptist, Paul's blinding light, and later the Kabbalah and Hasidic masters whose path to God runs through anguish. The Platonic Socrates of the Symposium and Phaedrus (wisdom arriving through the madness of love) and the medieval agreement of al-Ghazali, Maimonides, and Aquinas that reason cannot reach God frame his philosophy-versus-mysticism contrast, including the film's mother-son floorboard scene as love but not full mystical contact. The added scene where Pilate's wife tells him 'If you will not hear the truth, no one can tell you' shows Gibson siding with the mystical path to truth over Pilate's pragmatic one.

chapters.file: ch21 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
ch22 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Irwin takes Pilate's Quid est veritas as a guided tour of theories of truth applied to the film: Gibson's sympathetic Pilate embodies relativism, met with Nietzsche's 'truth is a woman' perspectivism and Baudrillard's postmodern laughter and rejected; Caiaphas and the bad thief demanding Jesus come down from the cross put the correspondence theory to work ('the proof is out there'), though beliefs hang on other beliefs ad infinitum; Simon of Cyrene's growing conviction models the coherence theory, exposed as necessary but not sufficient by Swinburne's case for versus Wells's case against the divinity of Jesus; and Pilate's Barabbas gambit parodies James's pragmatic theory, where working is not enough if there is no corresponding reality. He then retrieves Heidegger's reading of aletheia as uncovering, helped by the Quid est veritas anagram ('Est qui vir adest': it is the man before you) and Gadamer on truth seizing us like beauty, so that Jesus's 'I am the truth' and Claudia's dream-guided warnings point to truth as disclosure. Since disclosure alone cannot decide between inconsistent revealed claims, Irwin ends by leaving the viewer with a leap of faith and a first instinct as final answer.

holes.name: Peter Abelard
holes.what: Twelfth-century philosopher-theologian whose Moral Influence Theory understands Christ's death as the supreme revelation of God's love that awakens love in the sinner and transforms them morally.
holes.why: Chapter 12 presents Abelard's view as one of the three atonement theories Gibson's film weaves together (embodied in the transformed Mary Magdalene, Simon of Cyrene, the good thief, and the kneeling soldier) and defends it against the charge of neglecting objective guilt.

holes.name: Personalism
holes.what: The view, developed by Boston personalists like Bowne and Brightman and shared by thinkers from Buber to Scheler, that persons as such possess intrinsic, irreducible value that must never be subordinated to abstract ideals or to single aspects of persons like happiness.
holes.why: Chapter 13's entire argument, that Gibson's exclusive focus on the passion eclipses the whole person of Christ and risks relishing redemptive suffering, is explicitly grounded in the author's self-declared personalism.

holes.name: Catharsis (tragic purgation)
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics of tragedy as arousing pity and fear in order to cleanse them, achieved through a plot in which a flawed hero (hamartia) falls from prosperity.
holes.why: Chapter 14 tests The Passion against catharsis and hamartia, shows a flawless Christ cannot make an Aristotelian tragedy, and only then defends its violence as the Kantian sublime instead.

holes.name: Cinematic Verisimilitude
holes.what: The idea, associated with film theorist Andre Bazin, that photography's automatic, mind-independent recording of reality gives film unique credibility, which fictional narratives can exploit to pass as fact.
holes.why: Chapter 17 explains why Christian viewers take Gibson's slanted, Emmerich-based narrative as history: photographic realism transfers its evidential authority to the fiction, exactly as Griffith's Birth of a Nation did for the Klan.

holes.name: Religious Mysticism
holes.what: The view, classically analyzed by William James, that a higher truth can be accessed through a painful inner journey culminating in a direct, short-lived, ineffable experience of God that defies rationality.
holes.why: Chapter 20's whole argument reads Gibson's suffering Jesus as a Jewish mystic in the line of Moses, Elijah, Daniel, the Kabbalah, and Hasidism, using James's four marks of mystical experience as its analytic tool.

holes.name: Truth as Disclosure (aletheia)
holes.what: Heidegger's retrieval of the Greek aletheia: truth understood not as correspondence between proposition and fact but as uncovering or disclosing a new way for a world to show itself.
holes.why: Chapter 22 builds its final answer to Pilate's question on aletheia, reading Jesus's 'I am the truth', the veritas anagram, and Claudia's dreams as disclosure rather than criteria-based truth.

holes.name: Correspondence Theory of Truth
holes.what: The classic view that a proposition is true if and only if it matches the way things actually are.
holes.why: Chapter 22 applies it through Caiaphas's demand that Jesus come down from the cross as proof and The X-Files mantra 'the truth is out there', then objects that every verifying belief depends on further beliefs ad infinitum.

holes.name: Coherence Theory of Truth
holes.what: The view that a proposition is true if and only if it coheres consistently with the body of propositions already known to be true.
holes.why: Chapter 22 maps Simon of Cyrene's growing conviction onto coherence and shows via Swinburne versus G.A. Wells, and George Costanza's fabrications, that coherence is necessary but not sufficient for truth.
